## What Socket.IO is[​](#what-socketio-is "Direct link to What Socket.IO is")

Socket.IO is a library that enables **low-latency**, **bidirectional** and **event-based** communication between a client and a server.

![Diagram of a communication between a server and a client](/images/bidirectional-communication2.png)![Diagram of a communication between a server and a client](/images/bidirectional-communication2-dark.png)

The Socket.IO connection can be established with different low-level transports:

*   HTTP long-polling
*   [WebSocket](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSockets_API)
*   [WebTransport](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebTransport_API)

Socket.IO will automatically pick the best available option, depending on:

*   the capabilities of the browser (see [here](https://caniuse.com/websockets) and [here](https://caniuse.com/webtransport))
*   the network (some networks block WebSocket and/or WebTransport connections)

You can find more details about that in the ["How it works" section](/docs/v4/how-it-works/).

[`SUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/subscribe), [`UNSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/unsubscribe) and [`PUBLISH`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/publish) implement the [Publish/Subscribe messaging paradigm](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publish/subscribe) where (citing Wikipedia) senders (publishers) are not programmed to send their messages to specific receivers (subscribers).
Rather, published messages are categorized into channels, without knowledge of what (if any) subscribers there may be.
Subscribers express interest in one or more channels and only receive messages that are of interest, without knowledge of what (if any) publishers there are.
This decoupling of publishers and subscribers allows for greater scalability and a more dynamic network topology.

For instance, to subscribe to channels "channel11" and "ch:00" the client issues a [`SUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/subscribe) providing the names of the channels:

```bash
SUBSCRIBE channel11 ch:00
```

Messages sent by other clients to these channels will be pushed by Redis to all the subscribed clients.
Subscribers receive the messages in the order that the messages are published.

A client subscribed to one or more channels shouldn't issue commands, although it can [`SUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/subscribe) and [`UNSUBSCRIBE`](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/unsubscribe) to and from other channels.
The replies to subscription and unsubscribing operations are sent in the form of messages so that the client can just read a coherent stream of messages where the first element indicates the type of message.

## How it works[​](#how-it-works "Direct link to How it works")

The Redis adapter relies on the Redis [Pub/Sub mechanism](https://redis.io/topics/pubsub).

Every packet that is sent to multiple clients (e.g. `io.to("room1").emit()` or `socket.broadcast.emit()`) is:

*   sent to all matching clients connected to the current server
*   published in a Redis channel, and received by the other Socket.IO servers of the cluster

The Redis adapter assumes that Redis is part of the trusted internal infrastructure.

# [AMULET](https://www.amuletmc.com)

### Amulet is a Minecraft world editor and converter that supports every version since Java 1.12 and Bedrock 1.7

![python-logo-generic.png](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/048dc9_5068f62f83974e36ab6e9cf7a4ade904~mv2.png/v1/fill/w_327,h_97,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_avif,quality_auto/python-logo-generic.png)

Amulet is written in Python which means that you can manipulate world data with a bit of python knowledge.

​

The code behind Amulet is broken down into a number of parts to make it more modular.

​

Firstly there is [Amulet-Map-Editor](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-Map-Editor). This is the user interface that most users will interact with. Amulet Map Editor (usually shortened to just Amulet) has the ability to run code created by the user in the form of operations. These can be found in the operations tab of the 3D Editor. Users can create custom python programs placed in the 'plugins/operations' directory next to where the program is run from. The editor will display these in the operations list for the user to choose from. Note that you will need to press the refresh button within the operations tab to load/reload operations while the editor is running.

Some examples of the format can be found [here](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-Map-Editor/tree/master/amulet_map_editor/programs/edit/plugins/operations/examples) and the operations that are distributed with Amulet can be found [here](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-Map-Editor/tree/master/amulet_map_editor/programs/edit/plugins/operations/stock_plugins/operations).

​

Secondly there is [Amulet-Core](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-Core). This is a library which is used to manipulate the world data. A getting started guide and API documentation can be found on the [readthedocs page](https://amulet-core.readthedocs.io/en/latest/). If you plan to modify world data you will need to interact with this so it would be helpful to get familiar with it.

​

[PyMCTranslate](https://github.com/gentlegiantJGC/PyMCTranslate) is a library that handles block and biome translation between the different versions. It will in the future also support entity and item translation. This allows for data from a number of game versions to be edited interchangeably. This is also what enables Amulet to convert between the different world formats.

​

[Minecraft-Model-Reader](https://github.com/gentlegiantJGC/Minecraft-Model-Reader) is a library to parse resource packs and load the block models into a consistent format for easier use. The 3D Editor uses this to generate the terrain that is show to the user.

​

Finally is [Amulet-NBT](https://github.com/Amulet-Team/Amulet-NBT) which is a low level binary NBT and stringified NBT (SNBT) library. NBT is a storage system that most of Minecraft uses to save data. This exists to read and write that data. It is written in Cython to make it as fast as possible.

## Problems and contradictions in the README v2 sketch (resolve before coding)

These were found by re-reading the README closely. Implementing agents must not silently pick a side; each needs the decision recorded in `docs/v2/DECISIONS.md` (Step 0.4).

1. **Efficiency numbers don't match.** Text says centre = 100%, edge at distance 7,000 = 30%. The formula `max(30, 100 - distanz/200)` gives 65% at 7,000 and only hits the 30% floor at 14,000. The JS snippet `Math.max(30, 100 - d * 0.005)` is identical to `/200`, so the *text* is wrong, not the code. Decision needed: keep formula (floor at 14,000) or steepen to reach 30% at 7,000 (`100 - d/100`).
2. **World/chunk geometry is ambiguous.** "20000x20000 virtuelle Einheiten, aufgeteilt in 100x100 Chunks" can mean 100×100 = 10,000 chunks of 200×200 units, or chunks of 100×100 units = 40,000 chunks. This changes DB size, worker sharding (Phase 5 uses 1000x1000 areas), and the scatter algorithm. Must be fixed in one ADR before schema work.
3. **Scatter placement is unspecified.** "kein Grid, random verteilt, Wege dazwischen" — no algorithm, no minimum distance, no collision/retry rule, no determinism/seed. Needs a spec (e.g. Poisson-disc / jittered grid with min-distance and max-attempts + fallback) or chunk assignment will deadlock as the world fills.
4. **No identity/auth in the sketch.** "Beim ersten Login" assumes accounts, but no auth system, session, or anti-multi-account rule is defined. This blocks Phase 0 schema (`owner` in `bases`) and all of monetisation. Biggest missing decision in the plan.
5. **No economy model.** Buildings "produziert", server "prüft Ressourcen" — but resources, production rates, costs, offline production, and caps are undefined. Phase 2 cannot be built or balanced without a resource/building table first.
6. **Redis appears in Phase 3 before it's introduced.** Admin writes MariaDB + `redis.publish('chunk:update', …)`, but Redis is only justified later by multi-worker scaling. Decide: introduce Redis in Phase 0 (needed anyway for the Socket.IO adapter once >1 server process runs) or defer to Phase 5.
7. **Monetisation has no payment, legal, or ToS workstream.** Selling base slots/boosters (even cosmetics) needs a payment provider, refund/consumer law handling (DE/EU), and a decision on the booster-vs-"ohne Pay2Win" tension the README itself creates (paid efficiency booster at the edge is arguably pay-to-win). Flagged as a product decision, not an engineering task.
8. **Minecraft import licensing.** Importing "1000 SpigotMC Maps" raises map-author licence/redistribution rights. Needs a rights check per imported map before public placement, same class of risk as SECURITY_REVIEW finding 2.

## Approach

Build v2 as five gated phases exactly following the README's order (foundation → efficiency/placement → factories → admin → MC import → scaling/monetisation), but insert a **Phase 0.0 decision/spec gate** first, because contradictions 1–5 above make Phases 1–2 unbuildable as written. Each phase ships behind a feature flag / separate route so v1 on Vercel never breaks. Every phase ends with a playable or operable increment, automated tests, and a docs update, per [rules.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/rules.md) and [CONTRIBUTING.md](/C:/Users/danie/OneDrive/github-repos/stranded-horizons/CONTRIBUTING.md).

Suggested agent workstreams (for the owner's future multi-agent loop, one owner per stream, no two agents editing the same file concurrently):

- **Agent A — Server/Simulation:** `server/`, tick loop, chunk assignment, efficiency, factory rules.
- **Agent B — Client:** v2 Canvas client, world/chunk rendering, build UI, socket client; v1 files read-only.
- **Agent C — Data/Infra:** `db/` migrations, Docker Compose (MariaDB, Redis, server), KVM deploy, NGINX/WebSocket proxying, monitoring.
- **Agent D — Admin:** `admin/` panel, Leaflet live map, chunk editor, world events, in-game `:` console.
- **Agent E — MC Import:** `tools/mc-import/` Python service, `mc_to_sh.json`, preview generation.
- **Agent F — QA/Docs (rotating):** tests, `ASSETS_LICENSES.md`, README/rules sync, playtest checklists. Every phase PR requires F's checklist before merge.

### Phase 1 — Efficiency & faction links (README Phase 1)

1.1. `server/world.js`: single `getEfficiency(x, y)` implementing the 0.1-decided formula; unit tests pinning the worked table from 0.1 so formula and docs can never drift again.
1.2. Faction link flow: `link:request` → other owner gets pending request → `link:confirm`/`link:reject`; on confirm, both bases gain +10% efficiency, hard-capped at 100%, recomputed server-side; unlink removes the bonus. Store link state only in `faction_links`; never cache the bonus without recompute on read-after-write.
1.3. Client: show base efficiency, link state, pending requests; chunk colour scale documented in UI legend.
1.4. Abuse cases: self-link, duplicate link, linking a non-existent/offline owner, link spam (rate limit + one pending request per pair).

### Phase 2 — Factories (README Phase 2, Factorio-light)

2.1. Build grid: each chunk exposes a 20×20 grid; `place`/`remove`/`upgrade` socket intents validated server-side for ownership, grid bounds, occupancy, and resource cost. Every rejection returns a typed error from PROTOCOL.md.
2.2. Simulation tick (2s): production/consumption for Mine → Förderband → Fabrik chains, turret/wall as static state in v1 of this phase; all arithmetic server-side, persisted per tick with the D6 idempotency key; offline production computed from elapsed ticks on load, capped per 0.1 economy table.
2.3. Client build UI: palette, ghost preview, costs, production rates, chunk inventory; render only server-sent state (no client-side resource math beyond display formatting).
2.4. Anti-cheat pass: fuzz every mutating event with out-of-range coordinates, negative amounts, foreign chunk IDs, and replayed messages; server must reject all without state change.

### Phase 3 — Admin (README Phase 3)

3.1. `admin/` app with separate admin auth (allowlisted accounts + audit log on every write). Routes: `/admin/world` live Leaflet map (`CRS.Simple`, chunk rectangles coloured by efficiency, click → chunk detail), chunk JSON editor with schema validation before save, manual efficiency override (stored as override, visibly marked, audited), structure placement using the same server validation path as players.
3.2. World events: admin action that places N ruin/bunker structures into eligible old chunks; implemented as a normal server-side placement batch + Redis `chunk:update` publish so online workers reload affected chunks (MariaDB remains the truth; Redis is only a reload hint, at-most-once is acceptable because clients also re-fetch on reconnect).
3.3. In-game `:` console for admins only (server re-checks admin flag on every command): `:tp x y`, `:give <resource> <amount>`, `:place <type>`; every console action writes to `admin_audit`. Non-admin attempts are rejected and logged.
3.4. Safety: admin writes require confirmation for destructive actions, all admin endpoints behind the private network/VPN or IP allowlist in addition to auth, and a tested DB backup/restore runbook before admin goes live.

### Phase 4 — Minecraft import (README Phase 4)

4.1. `tools/mc-import/` Python service (owner's Python focus): upload of `.schematic`/`.schem`/`region/` via the admin panel only, stored quarantined, size/type limits, malware-safe handling (no execution of uploaded content).
4.2. Parser spike first: prove Amulet-Core can read one real Java world/region and one schematic from the owner's collection and enumerate blocks; if a format is unsupported, record it and descope that format rather than writing a hand parser.
4.3. `mc_to_sh.json` mapping (versioned, in-repo): start from the README's four mappings (stone→metal_wall, iron_block→factory_t1, chest→loot_container, spawner→enemy_spawner); unmapped blocks → explicit `ignore` or `unknown` bucket counted in the import report, never silently dropped.
4.4. Transform → blueprint JSON conforming to the Phase 2 building schema, with a 2D/3D preview in the admin panel; placement is a separate explicit admin action into a chosen chunk (as dungeon/ruin), reusing Phase 3 placement + audit. Imports never overwrite a player's base without an explicit override confirmation.
4.5. Rights gate: each imported map records source + licence/permission in `imports` and an `IMPORTS_LICENSES.md`; unlicensed maps stay in a private test world only.

### Phase 5 — Hosting, scale, monetisation (README Phase 5)

5.1. Sharding: partition the world into 1000×1000 areas, one worker container each, Socket.IO Redis adapter for cross-worker broadcast; infra automation starts a worker when its area exceeds 80% occupancy (metric defined in 0.3: assigned chunks / capacity). Load test must prove the 80% trigger before it is trusted.
5.2. Hardening & ops: backups (automated, restore-tested), monitoring/alerting on the owner's existing tooling, error tracking, tick-lag and socket-connection dashboards, incident runbook.
5.3. Monetisation (only after legal/product decisions in Risks): free base, paid 2nd base slot (one-time), cosmetics, edge efficiency booster (7 days, never above 100%) — implemented as entitlements on `users`, granted only by verified payment webhooks; no payment code before provider + EU consumer-law review.
5.4. Public launch gate: `ASSETS_LICENSES.md` complete (SECURITY_REVIEW finding 2), privacy policy/ToS live, data-export/delete for accounts, load test + 7-day closed beta with rollback plan (v1 remains live throughout).

## How self-hosted Supabase differs

Self-hosted Supabase runs as a single project, which means that Studio doesn't support multiple organizations or projects. Most settings are configured through [environment variables](https://github.com/supabase/supabase/blob/master/docker/.env.example).

Some features of the managed platform aren't available when self-hosting: branching, advanced metrics beyond logs, managed backups and PITR, analytics and [vector buckets](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/storage/vector/introduction), ETL, and the Management API. To collect logs and metrics yourself, see the community-maintained [observability project](https://github.com/supabase-community/supabase-observability).

### Not the same as local development

[Supabase CLI](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development/cli/getting-started) runs a local stack for development and testing. That stack is not a self-hosted deployment: it is not hardened for production and must not be exposed to external traffic.

To self-host, use [Docker](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/self-hosting/docker) or the community-maintained [Kubernetes project](https://github.com/supabase-community/supabase-kubernetes).

    const world_y = (cy - 50) * 200 + Math.random() * 200;
    const clash = await db.query(
      'select 1 from bases where power(world_x - $1, 2) + power(world_y - $2, 2) < power($3, 2) limit 1',
      [world_x, world_y, attempt < 25 ? 150 : 75]);
